newsitem.title: USA: U.S. pressing Saudi Arabia over religious freedom.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pressing Saudi Arabia over religious freedom.

text.p: The United States is pressing Saudi Arabia to permit U.S. officials to worship freely in the strictly Islamic kingdom, a senior U.S. official said on Thursday.
Assistant Secretary of State John Shattuck was speaking as the State Department published an annual human rights report that spotlighted lack of religious and other freedoms in Saudi Arabia.

"We have been very concerned and have raised both privately and publicly the issue of freedom of religion and particularly the question of the free exercise of religion by United States personnel when they are in Saudi Arabia," Shattuck said.

Shattuck, who oversaw publication of the worldwide report, told a news conference that the section on Saudi Arabia indicated "the difficulties of, in fact almost impossibilities of, exercising freedom of religion."

"I think our engagement on this subject is very important in terms of presenting a climate in which individuals from overseas are able to practice their faith," he said. "We are going to press to make sure that that is possible in the future as well."

Shattuck was speaking after Secretary of State Madeleine Albright announced that religious freedom around the world would be a new priority of U.S. human rights policy. She did not specifically mention Saudi Arabia.
The annual rights report stated that freedom of religion "does not exist" in Saudi Arabia, where public and private non-Moslem religious activities were banned.
It cited a case where a Christian service was broken up by police and religious vigilantes known as Mutawwa'in, and the man who hosted the service was punished by lashing.
The report did not specifically mention problems faced by U.S. personnel in Saudi Arabia who include some 5,000 troops as well as diplomatic staff.

Despite Washington's close political ties with Riyadh, the report was sharply critical of Saudi human rights practices, charging that the government "commits and tolerates serious human rights abuses."

It said Saudi security forces carried out arbitrary arrests and abused detainees. The government prohibited or restricted freedom of speech, the press, assembly and association as well as religion, it said.

The report said that after a five-month period without executions in Saudi Arabia they resumed March 15. By year's end the authorities had beheaded 66 men and three women for offences ranging from murder to witchcraft.

In a brief reference to a truck-bomb explosion that killed 19 U.S. servicemen near Dhahran on June 25, the report said Saudi authorities had "arrested dozens of people" but the investigation was continuing at year's end.
U.S. officials have complained recently of lack of information from the Saudis in the investigation.
